segments.say: Many people believe that habits, once formed, are set for life. That after a certain age, the brain is fixed, and change becomes impossible. William James himself wrote that habits set like plaster as we grow older. But modern neuroscience has found that the adult brain is more changeable than people once thought.

One famous line of research involves London taxi drivers. To get their license, they must learn what's called The Knowledge. The layout of thousands of streets and landmarks across the city. It can take years of study, riding around on scooters, memorizing routes. It's one of the most demanding memory tasks in any profession.

In two thousand, the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire and her colleagues compared brain scans of London taxi drivers with scans of people who weren't taxi drivers. And they found that a rear part of the hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory and navigation, tended to be larger in the taxi drivers. And it tended to be larger in drivers who had spent more years on the job.

show.where: University College London, published in PNAS, 2000
show.what: Brain scans of licensed London taxi drivers were compared with scans of people who were not taxi drivers.

segments.say: Later work, following trainees over time, suggested that this change appeared as people learned The Knowledge, rather than simply being something they were born with. Adult brains, learning and practicing intensely, seemed to physically change. This kind of change is often called neuroplasticity. The brain's ability to reshape itself through experience.

Neuroplasticity is generally strongest in childhood. But research suggests that it continues throughout life. Older adults can learn new skills, new languages, new instruments. It may take a little longer, and require more repetition. But the capacity to change remains.

For habits, this is good news. It means that it's never too late to build new routines, or loosen old ones. The same repetition that built your current habits can build new ones. At twenty, at fifty, at eighty. The brain keeps listening to what you repeat.

show.cap: Habits can change at any age.

segments.say: In some ways, older people may even have advantages. More self knowledge. A clearer sense of what matters. More experience of what works and what doesn't. Those insights can help in choosing the right cues, the right rewards, and the right pace. Change may be slower, but it can be wiser.

At the same time, old habits often leave traces. Research suggests that old habits may not completely disappear, but can be overridden by new ones. Under stress or in old contexts, they may reappear. That's not failure. It's just the old path, still visible in the grass. With time, the new path becomes the more worn one.

I like to picture habits as paths across a meadow. The old path is well worn, the grass flattened by years of walking. When you start a new path, it's barely visible. Walking it feels uncertain. But each day you walk it, it becomes a little clearer. And slowly, the old path grows over with grass, while the new one becomes the easy way home.

So whatever your age, and however long you've had a habit, your brain is still listening. Still learning. Still ready to be shaped by what you do next. That's one of the most hopeful facts in all of neuroscience. It's never too late.

So here's what we've learned about change at any age. London taxi drivers showed brain differences linked to years of learning. The adult brain keeps reshaping itself through experience. Habits can change at any age, though it may take patience. And new habits are like new paths in a meadow, slowly becoming the easy way home.
